title: Through the Lens of Pleasure: Joy-Centred Pedagogy Through Somatic and Arts-Based Engagements
abstract: In a time in which the academic world mirrors the challenges and crises of the wider world, we consider and advocate for joy-centred pedagogy. Studying three educational spaces under one departmental umbrella, we connect the sensual and experiential aspects of attuning to joy. We share the ways in which joy is not a destination. Rather, joy emerges in higher educational settings when we share in the practices that are connective and focused. We expound on three examples of joy-centred pedagogy in higher education: a sex-ed learning placement for pre-service teachers taught and experienced through the lens of pleasure and joy; joy/pleasure-centred bubble painting within an arts education research group; and a joy/pleasure-centred education graduate course where bodies push against the edge of AI. Themes such as experiential sensuous learning, care in community, and curiosity serve to help identify what incites joy in teaching and learning.

title: Teaching with Joy: Strategies for Students with Behavioural Difficulties
abstract: The current educational context, characterized by increasingly diverse learner profiles, makes classroom behaviour management particularly complex. Teachers face a wide range of challenges, from minor disruptions to more serious behavioural issues, which may negatively affect both classroom climate and the well-being of students and teachers. This study is based on a survey of 76 secondary school teachers from various disciplines who work with students exhibiting behavioural difficulties. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, combining qualitative and quantitative data. The study examines teachers’ classroom management strategies and their contribution to fostering a positive classroom climate, enhancing student engagement and motivation, and supporting emotional well-being and joy in learning. It also explores the effectiveness of teacher training, the challenges encountered, and the need for professional support, resources, and development. Based on the findings, the study proposes recommendations to support the development of an inclusive, joy-centred, and resilient pedagogy that promotes student flourishing and a positive learning environment. title: Play as a Climate-Shifting Pedagogy: Cultivating Joy and Engagement in Higher Education
abstract: Many faculty report increasing demands within higher education, including larger class sizes, pressure associated with the broader political climate, increasing student distress, and greater difficulty engaging students (APA, 2023; Boamah et al., 2022; Fernández-Suárez et al., 2021; Wiley, 2024). These conditions have been associated with increased stress and burnout among faculty (Boamah et al., 2022; Leiter & Maslach, 2004). These pressures may contribute to a tightening of classroom climates as instructors and students adapt to increasingly constrained learning environments. This article proposes playful pedagogy as one approach for shifting classroom conditions. I present the idea of overlapping climates (i.e., attentional, power and authorship, social and relational, and meaning-making climates) and describe how play can create climate shifts that positively influence how students experience learning and how instructors experience teaching. Tangible examples are given to show how play can loosen overly controlled environments, capture attention, and invite co-construction of meaning. As these conditions shift, engagement and joy become more likely. The joy that arises in class

title: Joy as Epistemic Energy: How Emotional–Epistemic Interactions Enhance Scientific Sense-Making, Conceptual Understanding, and Student Agency
abstract: Amid increasing student disengagement, emotional distress, and performance-driven science instruction, this paper examines joy-centred pedagogy as a critical mechanism for fostering students’ scientific sense-making and agency. Drawing on sociocultural and epistemic perspectives in science education, the study conceptualizes joy not as a peripheral emotional outcome but as an embodied, relational, and renewable epistemic resource that energizes learning. Using a mixed-methods design, data were collected from secondary science classrooms implementing inquiry-based, joy-centred instructional practices. Quantitative analyses examined the relationships among students’ experienced joy, scientific agency, epistemic engagement, and conceptual understanding, while qualitative data illuminated how joy emerged through collaborative inquiry, productive struggle, and engagement with uncertainty. Structural equation modelling revealed that joy significantly predicted students’ agency and epistemic engagement, which in turn mediated conceptual understanding. Qualitative findings further demonstrated that joy functioned as a form of collective care, enabling students to take intellectual risks, p

title: Cultivating Joy Through Making: A Joy-Centred Pedagogical Study of Makerspaces in Primary Education
abstract: This study examines how joy is cultivated in a primary school Makerspace through the implementation of joy-centred pedagogy. While innovative learning environments are often assumed to naturally generate positive emotional experiences, limited research has investigated the pedagogical conditions that intentionally foster joyful learning in primary education contexts. Grounded in experiential learning theory, positive psychology, self-determination theory, and maker education, the study adopts a design-based research approach to explore how structured learning experiences can support the emergence of joy during hands-on learning activities. The intervention was conducted in a primary school Makerspace where students engaged in collaborative project-based tasks involving design, experimentation, and iterative problem-solving. Data were collected through student surveys, classroom observations, and reflective artifacts and analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. The findings reveal that joy was cultivated through four interrelated pedagogical conditions: meaningful challenge, collaborative interaction, learner autonomy, and opportunities for creative expression. title: Cultivating Joy Through Inclusion: Teachers’ Practices Supporting Young Learners with Dyslexia in Zimbabwean Mainstream Classrooms
abstract: Amid persistent resource shortages and exclusionary instructional practices, learners with dyslexia in mainstream classrooms are often portrayed through deficit-focused narratives that emphasise struggle and remediation. This study examines how joy functions as a pedagogical tool within inclusive teaching strategies in Zimbabwean primary schools. The study adopted a qualitative design involving twenty-four (24) primary school teachers from Chivi District, selected through convenience sampling based on their experience teaching learners with dyslexia across Grades 1 to 7. Data were generated through classroom observations and semi-structured interviews, enabling an in-depth exploration of teachers’ practices and perspectives. Findings indicate that teachers can intentionally cultivate joy through relational care, adaptable instruction, and supportive learning environments. Joy was specifically fostered through multimodal teaching approaches, collaborative activities, and the normalisation of learner differences, allowing learners with dyslexia to engage meaningfully and experience success. These practices enhanced learner participation and agency while also strengthening teachers’ p

title: Cultivating Relational Joy: Integrating Self-Determination Theory with Joy-Centred Pedagogical Practice
abstract: This conceptual article explores joy as a relational and pedagogical force in higher education, examining its connection to student motivation, well-being, and belonging through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Drawing on SDT’s core psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, the paper argues that joy is best understood not simply as an individual emotional outcome but as an emergent property of learning environments that either support or frustrate these needs. From this perspective, joy arises in inclusive classroom communities shaped by shared learning, mutual care, and collective meaning-making, while its absence may reflect disconnection, constraint, or diminished competence. The paper further argues that cultivating joy-centred pedagogy is not only a matter of effective teaching but also an ethical responsibility, particularly in light of inequitable access to need-supportive educational environments. By connecting SDT with research on joy in education, this article offers a conceptual framework for understanding how educational environments shape the conditions under which joy becomes possible and identifies implications for educators and insti

title: Snippets of Connection: Collaborative Creativity as Joy-Centered Practice
abstract: This article examines collaborative creativity as a joy-centred practice that faculty can cultivate amid the pressures of academic life. Drawing on our own long-term collaboration as the primary site of inquiry, we define collaborative creativity as a relational, reiterative process through which meaning is co-constructed in response to the shared successes and challenges of faculty life, positioning struggle not as an individual burden but as an occasion for collective invention. Methodologically, we employed social reflection, thematic analysis, and poetry inquiry, with poems crafted from interview data functioning as both analytic tools and affective representations of snippets of connection. Our findings reveal joy as something that arises not through seeking it directly but through doing meaningful work together — and burnout as a systemic phenomenon that collaborative creativity interrupts by turning faculty outward, toward one another and toward the in-between spaces where curiosity and creativity quietly take hold. We conclude with invitations for faculty to take up collaborative creativity in their own professional lives, offering it not as a prescriptive model but as an h

title: Constructing Collective Joy: Slogans, Social Identity, and Extremism Prevention in Religious Education
abstract: Joy is increasingly recognized as a pedagogical resource that shapes identity, social relations, and psychological resilience. Grounded in the work of Ross Gay, joy is conceptualized not as a denial of hardship but as a relational experience cultivated through care, solidarity, and collective endeavor within educational spaces. However, empirical studies on how collective joy is mediated through organizational symbols—particularly among female students in value-based educational communities—remain scarce. This study examined how female students at Pondok Pesantren Salafiyah Syafi'iyah Situbondo construct their identity through organizational slogans and explored their affective experiences and behavioral orientations in the context of extremism prevention, through a joy-centered pedagogical lens. A phenomenological approach was employed with 40 female student participants selected via purposive and key informant sampling. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and analyzed through phenomenological description, horizontalization, thematic clustering, and essence formulation. Findings revealed four interconnected semantic clusters—sisterhood and radical inclusion, solidarity

title: The Delightful Unessay: How Learners’ Freedom to Choose an Assessment Modality Sparks Pedagogical Joy (Even in the Age of AI)
abstract: In this article, I argue that one of the principle ways that unessay assignments bring joy to college educators is by creating opportunities for us to work with students who are creatively and meaningfully engaging in our course content—the research fields and disciplinary tools of our own scholarly passions—using an assessment modality of their own choice. After an overview of what an unessay assignment entails, I describe how it facilitates unlearning passivity for students and unlearning didactic teaching and the transmission model of education for faculty. The unessay creates more freedom for learners to explore their own unique ideas and to find personally relevant meaning in an academic subject, making teaching with unessays an intellectually and pedagogically rewarding, even joyful, task for professors—something we all need more of in “the age of AI.”

title: Sharing the Tea: Warming Up the Classroom in Cold Times
abstract: As evidenced by the grim gazes and demeanors of students as they quietly settle into their seats for the day, the Polycrisis, defined as the “…multiple co-occurring, causally entangled crises with synergistic and cascading effects on multiple systems degrading humanity’s prospects…” (Rakowski et al., 2025), is clearly infecting, exacerbating, and curdling the potential of our young people trying to carve their way through an increasingly unstable world. In the face of such iron frost upon the world stage, educators have a genuine opportunity to reinvigorate hope and joy for learning by thawing the perceptual chill with pedagogical practices that enflame warmth and laughter within the classroom. To this end, I will draw on empirical evidence supporting embodied cognition, highlighting the sociocultural interplay between physicality and mental states (Macrine & Fugate, 2022) to illustrate what I call ‘Cozy Pedagogy’. This novel form of classroom community building includes practices such as sharing tea from around the world with students in order to infuse warmth and wellbeing into our classroom dynamics, building new and lasting relationships for collective resilience.

title: Cultivating Joy through Translanguaging Pedagogy: Inclusion and Justice in Multilingual Classrooms in Pakistan
abstract: Abstract Using a qualitative multiple-case study design, this study examines how joy-centred translanguaging pedagogy promotes inclusion and justice in multilingual ESL classrooms in Pakistan. Grounded in the framework of translanguaging space, the study draws on classroom observations and semi-structured interviews with 2 teachers and 4 students. The analysis focuses on linguistic belonging, participation, language hierarchies, and student voice. Findings indicate that translanguaging supports identity validation and engagement; however, its effectiveness depends significantly on teachers’ affective and relational practices. Classrooms characterized by empathy, respect, and supportive feedback enabled greater student participation and a stronger sense of belonging. The study concludes that inclusion and justice emerge through the intersection of translanguaging practices and positive classroom relationships, positioning joy as central to equitable multilingual pedagogy.

title: Listening Towards Joy: Journalistic Learning and the Civic Possibilities of Writing Pedagogy in Teacher Education
abstract: Academic writing instruction often positions argumentation and persuasion as the primary modes of civic discourse, reinforcing adversarial forms of public discourse beyond the classroom. This article argues that writing pedagogy centred on joy can reimagine civic writing, orienting it toward relational learning, ethical representation, and writing as a way of being (Yagelski, 2009) rather than writing designed “to persuade, to argue, to win” (Neville, 2023, p. 94). Drawing on practitioner inquiry and a world-building civic education framework, this study examined how teacher candidates engaged in journalistic learning as a third space (Gutierrez et al., 1995; Moje et al., 2009) to bridge school and out-of-school literacies. Findings show that listening—requiring participants to suspend assumptions and attend carefully to others—reshaped beliefs and relational habits for teacher candidates. Joy emerged not despite this labour, but because of it, signaling deep engagement and pointing toward more ethical, relational civic futures.

title: Black Male Principals and Joy-Centred Leadership; Finding “Possible Joy” in the Impossible Search for Mattering in K-12 Spaces
abstract: Black school leaders are exemplars of joy-centered leadership that is needed in schools today. K-12 principals face unprecedented challenges in the post-COVID era. Specifically, Black male principals experience extreme challenges due to deficit framing that has informed hiring and retention practices, promotion, job roles and job-related stress unique to Black male principals. Despite these challenges, the Black principals in this collective case study demonstrated a “possible joy” approach to leadership while experiencing marginal mattering (minimal recognition; insignificance) and partial mattering (selective mattering based on talent/skills) in K-12 spaces. In this article, the author conceptualizes “possible joy” as a confluence of dispositions and characteristics comprised of tenets from Black joy and Black masculine caring. The data analysis revealed themes of “possible joy” through resistance, care for students, and leadership rooted in core values and conviction. Implications for K-12 administrators and educational leadership programs are discussed.

title: Happiness as a Component of Recovering Motivation and Resiliency in Disaster-Prone Philippine Academic Settings
abstract: While educational disaster response typically prioritizes infrastructure restoration, there remains a critical deficit in psychosocial interventions that cultivate joy to address recurrent climate trauma. This study investigates the utility of happiness dispositions (joy, humour, satisfaction) as culturally mediated pedagogical resources for recovering academic motivation and resiliency among learners in disaster-prone regions. Using a qualitative exploratory design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 tertiary students selected via purposive sampling in high-risk zones, and analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. Findings reveal that a joyful classroom climate is a vital foundational element. Establishing psychological safety acts as a catalyst, shifting students' neurobiology out of "survival mode" and freeing cognitive resources for learning. Emergent themes indicate culturally grounded humour and teacher relatability function as cognitive scaffolds for emotional anchoring. Aligning positive affect with academic material enhances retention while deconstructing fear-based academic hierarchies. This relational process, rooted in kapwa (shared identity), allows

title: Interdisciplinarity and the Epistemic Conditions of Pedagogical Joy
abstract: Joy-centred pedagogy has gained recent traction as educators seek alternatives to cynicism, disengagement, and burnout. Yet much of the existing discourse considers joy as an affective or motivational outcome rather than a condition grounded in epistemology. This paper offers a theoretical analysis of joy-centred pedagogy through a lens of interdisciplinarity in education (Babich, 2020), positioning interdisciplinarity not as a curricular arrangement but as an epistemological orientation that resists the fragmentation and proceduralization of knowledge common in modern educational systems. Drawing on the Systematic Oppression of Knowledge and Epistemology (SOKE), this paper argues that epistemic fragmentation produces forms of alienation that foreclose the emergence of pedagogical joy. In contrast, interdisciplinary ways of knowing reintegrate meaning, agency, and relational understanding, creating conditions under which joy can emerge as an epistemic consequence rather than a pedagogical technique. By synthesizing interdisciplinarity and joy-centred pedagogy, this paper reframes joy as an outcome of epistemic coherence and agentic engagement. Furthermore, this analysis provides a

title: Resonance and Joy: A Pedagogical Relationship
abstract: The world we currently experience is characterized by acceleration and change. Western ideals of individualistic success, along with surrounding social structures, leads to alienation (Rosa, 2019). The purpose of education is to prepare students for the world they will encounter, but what world? We argue that rather than preparing students for a disconnected world focused on the individual, instead we aim for students to contribute to a changing future with a foundation of resilience, belonging, and connection. Hartmut Rosa (2019) has proposed the concept of resonance as a counterpoint to alienation – as an alert and present willingness to enter dialogue with the world. This view of presence has relevance to pedagogy through joy: joy becomes essential for resilience in an alienating age. This essay explores how Rosa’s concept of resonance can provide a conceptual architecture for a joy-centred pedagogy. Drawing on Ross Gay's work on joy and its interaction with Rosa, we suggest that resonant pedagogical encounters create a reciprocal relationship with joy: an emergent quality of relational, dialogical, and meaningful engagements. We argue that resonance-oriented learning environmen

title: Patches of Joy: Reimagining Teacher Agency Through Art-Informed Inquiry
abstract: Joy-centred pedagogy is often dismissed as an “add-on” to serious teaching; however, in deficit-driven policy climates, educators increasingly describe schooling as scripted, dehumanizing, and joyless. This qualitative study examines how joy can be intentionally cultivated in teacher education as an embodied resource for agency, justice, and sustainability. Situated within narrative a/r/tography, this research draws on arts-informed inquiry in a graduate-level teacher education course in which participants created collage-based “patches and quilts” to render their teaching identities through visual metaphor and written reflection. Analysis of this multimodal corpus revealed four interrelated dimensions of joy as both affect and action: (a) inward renewal through reflective identity work; (b) refusal and navigation amid systemic constraints, including high-stakes testing and prescriptive curricula; (c) justice-oriented commitments, including Black joy and culturally sustaining approaches to language and culture; and (d) enacted pedagogy through practices that centre student voice, belonging, and creative, critical literacies. Findings suggest that arts-based inquiry creates a third-

title: I Stopped Managing Students and Started Facilitating Humans: Recalibrating Teaching in Higher Education
abstract: This reflective practitioner essay examines joy-centered pedagogy by shifting from classroom management to classroom facilitation in higher education. Drawing on embodied teaching practice, it considers the limitations of management frameworks rooted in K–12 schooling and the need to recalibrate pedagogy when working with emerging and seasoned adult learners. Across academic levels, students struggled with autonomy, accountability, reflection, and instructional follow-through, underscoring that developmental readiness does not automatically align with institutional expectations. Rather than responding with greater structure or tighter control, the essay argues for joy-centered facilitation as a pedagogical stance grounded in care, empathy, agency, and shared responsibility. Within this framework, joy is understood not as ease or positivity, but as an embodied pedagogical resource activated through curiosity, relational trust, and the permission to struggle, fail, and grow. Teaching life skills alongside disciplinary thinking became essential, as did relinquishing performative authority in favor of reciprocal learning. Guided by the principle “if you don’t bend, you’ll break,” this

title: The Joy of Authenticity in the College Composition Classroom in the Age of AI
abstract: Many conversations about generative AI in the classroom often demonstrate a deficit mindset toward students, with assumptions that AI has led to students never completing their own assignments or having their own creative thoughts. As a university writing instructor, I have found these concerns to be largely unfounded. My students are finding their own authentic voices and producing original work, while using AI as a tool to help them meet learning outcomes in ways that comply with university research ethics. In the era of AI—when assignments, thoughts, and opinions can be easily outsourced to generative AI—it is critical that students understand the importance and value of having their own original thoughts and opinions, and the dangers of outsourcing them to an algorithm. Yet, encouraging students to find and use their own authentic voices through a well-developed curriculum, one that both fosters student self-efficacy and incorporates ethical use of AI, can be a joyful endeavour for an instructor, as it ultimately leads to joy for students. This article introduces collegiate-level curricular activities, some involving the use of AI, that help foster the development of authentic

title: AI Agents, Joyful Assessment, and Third Space: Rethinking Assessment in the GenAI Era
abstract: This paper argues that assessment reform in the generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) era should move beyond defensive approaches focused primarily on preventing misconduct or detecting AI use. Synthesizing scholarship on assessment validity, relational and compassionate assessment, third space theory, and AI agents, this conceptual paper proposes joyful assessment as a rigorous and learner-centered framework for assessment design in the GenAI era. Joyful assessment is defined as assessment that is safe, emotionally responsive, empowering, and supportive of student agency. The paper examines how AI agents designed for specific educational purposes can support joyful assessment by creating low-stakes opportunities for practice, feedback, reflection, personalization, and multimodal demonstration of learning. It further argues that when implemented within relational and ethically governed environments AI agents can help mediate third space assessment environments that connect formal curriculum with students’ interests, experiences, and learning needs. The paper demonstrates these ideas through a practical example and concludes by identifying ethical considerations and future rese

title: Civic Joy: Making Space for Joyful Classroom Conversations
abstract: Civic joy emerges in classrooms in which students practice mutual recognition and collective meaning-making. It offers an alternative to nihilism and apathy, generating not consensus or sameness but a sense of belonging. Making space for civic joy in political and civic education settings does not require professors to be entertaining or fun, but to allow students to discuss topics of real concern to them in ways that allow them to prioritize their membership in a shared world. Civic joy offers students a taste of being in a democratic community, directly benefiting students and indirectly benefiting democracy.

title: Exploring Joy Through Co-Creation: Reflections on Student-Led Course Design
abstract: Joy in higher education is often treated as incidental, yet it can be intentionally cultivated through the design of the learning environment, particularly via student–faculty co-creation. Drawing on a redesigned undergraduate Positive Psychology course, this work examines how involving students as partners in shaping the syllabus, assessments, and participation structures transforms the emotional and intellectual climate of the classroom. Rather than framing joy as entertainment or ease, it is conceptualized as relational and emergent, arising through agency, trust, shared responsibility, and productive struggle. Four key conditions supporting the emergence of joy are identified: consequential voice, shared responsibility, relational trust, and engagement through difficulty. Evidence from both student and instructor reflections illustrates how co-creation shifts learning from compliance to commitment and from isolation to community. While tensions remain, co-creation is presented as a practical and adaptable pedagogical framework. Joy, in this context, becomes a renewable resource that signals meaningful engagement and underscores the need to rethink classroom structures in respon

title: From Abstract to Alive: Joy-Centred Professional Development for Teaching Genetics in Secondary Schools
abstract: Traditional approaches to teaching genetics in life sciences have often failed to equip teachers with effective strategies for engaging learners with complex and abstract concepts. In contexts marked by teacher burnout, learner disengagement, and persistent conceptual difficulty, there is a growing need for professional development approaches that empower teachers with effective teaching and learning strategies. This article explores joy-centred pedagogy as a suitable approach to professional development of life sciences teachers through a university–school partnership. Guided by Placed-Based Education Theory, the study examines how outdoor, community-based teaching strategies supported teachers’ understanding of genetics and revitalized their pedagogical practice. The professional development initiative involved demonstrations and hands-on learning in a local garden and cattle kraal, where teachers engaged in simulations of genetic crosses using natural materials and observed inherited characteristics in cattle. A qualitative design employed purposive sampling of 20 Grade 10–12 life sciences teachers. The thematic analysis of data revealed renewed confidence, heightened motivation

title: Introducing Joy-Centered Pedagogy: Hope for Hard Times
abstract: My call for submissions for this special issue began with the unjoyful: an acknowledgement of global environmental collapse, political polarization, social breakdown, the threat of artificial intelligence eclipsing human thought…students who seem lonelier, more disengaged, dysregulated, and depressed than ever. I proceeded to pose the question: How can educators respond to this moment? I noted one reaction might be to throw our collective hands up in despair and retreat into cynical silence: “there’s nothing we can do; we tried, and we’re tired.” However, I asserted there is another way: joy-centred pedagogy. In his essay collection Inciting Joy, Ross Gay (2022) observed “joy is not separate from pain,” before he queried: “What if joy, instead of refuge or relief from heartbreak, is what effloresces from us when we help each other carry heartbreak?” Inspired by this wisdom, the concept of joy-centred pedagogy emerged during the development of a book I edited, Joy-Centered Pedagogy in Higher Education: Uplifting Teaching and Learning for All (Routledge, 2025). That publication articulated a necessary ‘next step’ beyond culturally-responsive and trauma-informed teaching to show ways

title: Joy for Whom? Joy to What End? The Promise and Peril of Joy-Centred Pedagogy
abstract: In this essay, we trouble the notion of joy in teaching and learning. We trouble it because we do not want to offer another status quo, shiny intervention grounded in hegemonic hierarchy. We trouble it because we want to explore how to co-narrate joy in a way that lets us, our colleagues, and our students realize our “magical” capacity, to borrow Sylvia Wynter’s word. Writing as three educators in a single analytic voice, with first-person narratives in which our standpoints diverge, we ask: joy for whom, to what end, and at what cost? We enter through the debate over generative AI because it reveals how students and educators are often positioned as objects of policy. Drawing on Sara Ahmed, Achille Mbembe, and Lauren Berlant, we examine how institutional calls for joy, if not critically interrogated, can function as affective governance, shifting responsibility for structural conditions onto individuals and their emotional performance. We then read joy through traditions that have long refused to separate it from struggle–Black and abolitionist thought, Chicane and Latina thought, and West and North African Sufi teachings. We close with questions, rather than how-to’s, that invite

title: The Applied Studio Model in Higher Music Education: Critical Perspectives and Opportunities
abstract: The Applied Studio Model in Higher Music Education: Critical Perspectives and Opportunities engages with the dominant one-to-one master-apprentice model in higher music education. The volume contextualises studio teaching in relation to current discussions about learner-centred pedagogy, assessment, pedagogy, professionalism, and the sociocultural dimensions of equity and responsibility. In this book the authors consider the relationality of care, the pedagogy of professionalism, the authority of teaching, the internationalization of student support, the assessment of, for, and as learning, the inclusive access to and structural inequities of sociocultural studio practice innovation, and gender pedagogies in vocal pedagogy. The applied studio is pedagogy, not merely a pedagogical tradition. It is a site of practice that requires the accountability of the institution, and the pedagogy demands an ongoing engagement of scholarly practice. While the majority of the discussions are situated in a Western higher education context, the book offers a research-based and ethically defensible re-imagining of studio teaching in the current landscape of higher music education.

title: Teaching and Learning Statistics: Concept Maps and Patterns that Connect
abstract: For many students in graduate programs of study, an introductory statistics course is often required but can bring anxiety and disconnection, as well as a perception that the discipline is abstract and challenging for students to integrate with their own academic knowledge. To address these concerns, this paper considers an approach to teaching and learning statistics, namely, collaborative concept maps. Drawing upon scholarly literature in statistical education, concept mapping, and complexity theory, this paper argues for a view of statistics classrooms as complex systems that self-organize and emerge through interaction, a diversity of ideas, and shared meaning-making, resulting in “patterns that connect.” To facilitate productive and meaningful connections, small randomized groups of students are invited to collaborate on concept maps as productive pedagogical structures to foster connections among conceptual concepts, the course text, other learning materials, and the learners themselves. To this end, this paper offers a theoretically- and conceptually-informed account of a pedagogical design that illustrates how collaborative concept mapping can function as a generative learn

title: Towards Artifactual Literacies: A Content Analysis of Secondary School History Curricula in Canada
abstract: The literature recognizes the benefits of teaching with artifacts, but questions about how artifacts might be situated within curricula and with what implications arise. To explore these questions within a settler-colonial context, this study conducted a content analysis of programmatic history curricula in Canada, focusing on teaching the World Wars with artifacts. Informed by an orientation of artifactual literacy and a collaborative research protocol guided by an Indigenous cultural educator, the study found that programmatic curricula call for the use of artifacts but provide a dearth of guidance on how artifacts might be conceptualized or the literacy or pedagogical requirements for making meaning with them. The study recommends that programmatic curricula include teaching and learning with artifacts and do so within a framework that acknowledges artifactual literacies and provides support for the ethical use of artifacts with special attention to responsibilities in a settler-colonial context.

title: AI-Powered Language Teaching: Transforming the Future of TESOL
abstract: This book provides a timely and comprehensive examination of how generative artificial intelligence is reshaping the field of TESOL and second language education. It introduces the core or foundational principles of generative AI as well as critically explores its capacity to transform language teaching, learning, and assessment practices. The early chapters situate these developments within the historical evolution of TESOL theories and methodologies, effectively demonstrating how AI aligns with and extends existing pedagogical approaches. As the discussion progresses, the book offers a detailed analysis of contemporary applications, including AI-driven tools such as virtual tutors, language learning platforms, and automated assessment systems. These are not presented uncritically; rather, they are examined through empirical studies and illustrative case examples that highlight both their pedagogical potential and practical limitations. The author pays particular attention to how educators and institutions can integrate such technologies in ways that are both effective and responsible. Importantly, the work engages with a range of pressing issues, including ethics, privacy, bias,

title: Exploring the Evolution of Personal Learning Environments: A Thematic Review
abstract: This manuscript presents a bibliometric analysis of personal learning environments (PLEs) over 25 years, drawing on 494 documents from 318 sources. Three scientometric software programs were used in data analysis: VOSviewer, Bibliometrix, and Publish & Perish. It reveals a steady growth in the field, with an average annual increase of 5.7% in publications and an average document age of 8.9 years, indicating a blend of current and historical research. Spanish universities stood out as leading institutions in PLE research, suggesting Spain's pivotal role in advancing the field, possibly due to funding, policy, or a robust scientific community. Spain ranked first in the frequency of contributions to PLE research, followed by Italy, Portugal, Finland, Switzerland, and France. Two influential publications in e-learning were highlighted: interactive learning environments from the UK and digital education review from Spain. New and fundamental keywords and emerging research areas were identified and categorized into leading clusters and types. This process enhances the understanding of the subject matter and facilitates the exploration of novel avenues for future inquiry. The research fin

title: Risk and Trust: The Lonely Journey of EFL Remote Teachers’ Integration of AI
abstract: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into 21st-century education has attracted significant attention, particularly in teaching English as a Foreign Language (EFL) in remote areas. This study explores the integration of risk and trust among EFL teachers in Indonesia as they incorporate AI tools into their teaching practices. Using a qualitative case study approach, the research focuses on two remote EFL teachers in Jambi, Indonesia, with at least four years of experience using AI. The data collection method included semi-structured interviews and teaching artifacts, focusing on AI integration, risk, and trust. This study employed thematic analysis to examine the data and identify the key themes in the perspectives of remote EFL teachers. The findings reveal that AI significantly enhances teaching preparation, streamlining tasks, tailoring learning materials, and analyzing student progress. Trust in AI, influenced by its usability, adaptability, and perceived benefits, plays a pivotal role in its successful adoption. However, notable risks accompany these merits, including over-reliance on AI, which may reduce critical thinking and creativity, as well as privacy and data security

title: Self-Empowerment and Academic Success: CliftonStrengths in Doctor of Physical Therapy Students
abstract: Leadership is vital in healthcare, improving patient care through quality, safety, and accountability. This study aimed to identify common CliftonStrengths themes among Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) students, to explore correlations with GPA, and to assess students' perceptions of their strengths. A retrospective, mixed-methods study was conducted with 121 DPT students. CliftonStrengths assessments were administered, and quantitative data were analyzed for common strengths and GPA correlations. Qualitative data explored student perceptions. The most common strengths were Restorative, Achiever, Relator, Learner, and Harmony. Command, Context, Maximizer, and Self-assurance were the least common. Relationship-building was the most frequent domain, influencing the least. No significant correlation was found between strengths domains and GPA, though students in the Executing domain had the highest average GPA (3.41) and those in Influencing the lowest (3.04). Findings align with those of other healthcare studies, in which Learner, Relator, and Achiever are common strengths. title: Transitions to School: Perspectives and Experiences from Latin America
abstract: The book "Transitions to School: Perspectives and Experiences from Latin America" introduces readers to the importance of understanding educational transitions in this diverse region. In the Latin American context, the transition from early childhood education to primary education is a crucial phase that has a direct impact on the development of Latin children. The book presents diverse perspectives and experiences that reveal the challenges and successes in supporting children through this significant change.

title: Assessing Teaching Competencies in Pre-Service Teachers: Design and Validation of INDUCTEACHING Instrument
abstract: Induction is a priority action during initial teacher training. This period should include formative training and assessment that allows the student teacher to reflect on their progress and the acquisition of teaching skills. This article presents the design (following a descriptive-inferential method of quantitative approach) and validation of the self-assessment instrument for teaching competencies INDUCTEACHING, developed ad hoc, within the framework of an induction proposal, with the participation of 19 education professionals - nine teachers from five universities who teach teacher training courses for preschool, primary and secondary school teachers and 10 teachers from six public schools - and a pilot test of the tool (in pre and post phases) with the participation of nine teachers in training in the last year of the Primary Education Degree during their training practices. The results demonstrate the tool's content validity and internal consistency and indicate an improvement in perceived mastery of competency between the pre- and post-phases, particularly in the analysis and reflection dimensions. It is observed that induction processes improve professional teaching skills

title: Democracy in the Classroom: 'It’s All About Participation'
abstract: This article investigates teachers’ conceptions of democracy, citizenship, and participation in Norwegian upper secondary vocational education and training (VET). While there is ample research on students’ understanding of democracy, less research has focused on how teachers understand the concept. Democracy and citizenship are among three interdisciplinary topics in Norway’s LK20 curriculum, and participation has a central place in both the curriculum and the Education Act, making this study both timely and important in the Norwegian context. This paper examines how the participating teachers understood the concepts of democracy, citizenship, and participation, their teaching of those concepts, and their classroom instruction. This qualitative study draws upon six semi-structured interviews with teachers working in an upper secondary school, whose principal recruited three female and three male teachers of common-core subjects in vocational study programs. The data were analyzed through meaning compression. title: Critical Dialogue: Navigating Internationalization and Invisible International Students in Canadian Higher Education
abstract: This critical dialogue employed critical multiculturalism and critical internationalization as overarching theoretical frameworks and uncovered continuous and on-going struggles for invisible international students and racialized nonnative English-speaking educators in English for Academic Purposes programs in Canadian Higher Education context. Utilizing duo-ethnographic method, the two EAP educators’ dialogues uncover ongoing struggles in English language education in English speaking countries, specifically in Canada including Native and Nonnative English Speaker Dichotomy in English language teaching and learning, Deficit Mindset, Racial Microaggressions, lack of institutional and systemic supports for the invisible international ELL students. We are calling for actions in policy and institutional support for all international students to create truly inclusive teaching and learning environments.

title: Pedagogy of Care Equipped International Post-Secondary Students to Thrive in Times of Post-Pandemic Crisis
abstract: According to several national indices and post‑pandemic surveys, post‑secondary international students remain at high risk for chronic stress and declining mental health. We therefore proposed a multidisciplinary study to examine the impact of a remote, modular intervention program across three wellness domains: 1) Social, 2) Emotional, and 3) Professional Learning (SEPL). These domains were selected to identify areas in which students might benefit most from targeted support. The SEPL modules were designed to help students: Social (S): learn how to network differently through virtual coffee chats to strengthen socio‑emotional connectedness; Emotional (E): openly share fears and anxieties related to educational uncertainty, work‑related stress, and experiences of discrimination; and Professional Learning (P): invest in personal and professional development, continue job searching, and engage in academic or extracurricular activities to build resilience and support ongoing learning. title: In-Service Teaching, Artificial and Digital Technologies, and Teacher Education
abstract: In this issue, we focus on in-service teaching, artificial and digital technologies, teacher education, and several additional topics. We begin with four articles on in-service education. They investigate the impact of repeated video-based self-reflection on the development of reflective practice among in-service English language teachers, a content analysis of programmatic history curricula in Canada, focusing on teaching the World Wars with artifacts, how teachers understand the concepts of democracy, citizenship, and participation, and how teachers structure classroom instruction, self-assessment and reflection strategy. We then share three articles on artificial and digital technologies. The articles examine the potential synergy between AI and non-AI tools, the integration of risk and trust among EFL teachers as they incorporate AI tools into their teaching practices, and a bibliometric analysis of personal learning environments. Then, we present two articles on teacher education. title: Multiethnographic Faculty Perspectives on Navigating Writing Support for Students in Higher Education in the Age of GenAI
abstract: We are a research collective of nine higher education educators and researchers discussing our perspectives on the impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools on the provision of academic writing support to students in higher education. Using a collaborative multiethnographic approach, we employ a narrative writing style that reflects a dialogic approach to our critical reflections on our personal experiences with GenAI within our unique contexts. Our perspectives are examined through the conceptual lenses of positive psychology (MacIntyre et al., 2016) and emotion labour and feeling rules (Benesch, 2018). The ensuing conversation invites our readers to consider with us three questions related to the impact of GenAI in higher education and on student academic writing: how our provision of writing support has changed, what concerns us about GenAI-mediated writing, and what promising practices are being used to incorporate GenAI tools as support for student writing into our pedagogy.
